plan.angle: Orforglipron (Foundayo): what to expect when starting the once-daily pill, from the US prescribing information and Medication Guide only. First sentence: name orforglipron and give the short answer. Then a 'you' scenario. At 20–30 s, quote the label's exact wording that the tablet can be taken any time of day without food or water restrictions, with no comparison to other pills. Chapters: (1) the label's exact indication and population, plus 'not with other GLP-1 medicines'; (2) how to take it, label wording only, no doses or titration; (3) common GI side effects as label-table rates vs placebo, plus the label's timing wording; (4) untagged comfort tips, including fluids unless told to limit them; (5) ATTAIN-1 results as 72-week averages in adults without diabetes, then a one-line re-hook: a Phase 3 sleep apnea result was published in JAMA on Nov 9, it isn't an approved use, and a planned filing isn't approval; (6) warnings in label wording: boxed thyroid warning and MTC/MEN 2 contraindication, pancreatitis, gallbladder, dehydration and kidney, low blood sugar with insulin or sulfonylureas, plus one line on NAION quoted from the label if it's there, otherwise credited to the FDA's Nov 9 Drug Safety Communication; (7) questions for your prescriber, including 'tell them every medicine you take'. Scoped don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice' and the prescriber line, spoken and on screen. Title suggestion: 'Orforglipron (Foundayo): What to Expect on the Pill' (≤50 characters, fine). Thumbnail: pill bottle plus 'FIRST MONTH?'.

Orforglipron (Foundayo) was FDA-approved on 1 Apr 2026 for chronic weight management in adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, alongside diet and activity. Sources: FDA approval letter https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2026/220934Orig1s000ltr.pdf and Lilly Medical https://medical.lilly.com/us/products/answers/is-foundayo-orforglipron-approved-and-is-it-available-309937. The label has a boxed thyroid C-cell tumour warning and contraindications for MTC/MEN 2, and it says not to use it with other GLP-1 RAs. Four fixes are needed. (a) The angle calls the 20–30 s payoff 'the label's no food or water timing rule'. That's ambiguous and could be scripted backwards. Foundayo is taken once a day at any time, without food or water restrictions, unlike oral semaglutide (Rybelsus), which has a fasting rule. Quote the label's Dosage and Administration wording exactly and don't contrast it with Rybelsus numbers. (b) The FDA's Nov 9 Drug Safety Communication requires every GLP-1 RA label to add NAION to Warnings and Precautions. Sources: https://www.optometrytimes.com/view/fda-now-requiring-naion-warning-across-glp-1-receptor-agonist-class and https://www.healio.com/news/ophthalmology/20261109/fda-to-require-naion-risk-warning-for-glp1-therapies. The Foundayo label may not be updated yet. Viewers will have seen the news, so don't leave it out. If the label isn't updated, credit one calm line to the FDA communication, not the label. (c) Move the sleep apnea hook out of the opening 30 s. A topic that doesn't match the title is our worst retention pattern (Strength opened at 41%). Put it in chapter 5 or just before the ending as a re-hook, saying it isn't an approved use and that a planned filing isn't approval. (d) Per-arm adverse-reaction rates from the label table are fine, but they must not turn into a dose or titration schedule. Name the arms the way the table does and give no step-up timing. Also add the label's drug-interaction and other-medicines points as a plain 'tell your prescriber about every medicine you take' line. ATTAIN-1 results stay framed as 72-week averages in adults without diabetes.

package.description:
Quick answer: Foundayo (orforglipron) is a once-daily GLP-1 tablet, FDA-approved in April 2026 for chronic weight management in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, alongside diet and activity. The label says one tablet a day, with or without food. In the 72-week ATTAIN-1 trial in adults without diabetes, average weight loss was 7.5% of body weight (lowest dose) to 11.2% of body weight (highest dose) vs 2.1% on placebo, counting everyone who started.

Severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting (possible pancreatitis): stop taking it and call your healthcare provider right away. Swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing, or a severe rash (serious allergic reaction): stop taking it and get medical help right away. For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop, switch or change your medicine on your own. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Sources:
1. FOUNDAYO Prescribing Information and Medication Guide, Eli Lilly (revised 7/2026): https://uspl.lilly.com/foundayo/foundayo.html
2. Lilly Medical, Is Foundayo (orforglipron) approved and is it available? (2026): https://medical.lilly.com/us/products/answers/is-foundayo-orforglipron-approved-and-is-it-available-309937
3. Wharton S, et al. N Engl J Med 2025 (ATTAIN-1): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40960239/

script.hook_pattern: Direct question with the answer first. Sentence 1 names orforglipron and the viewer's question, and the short answer is spoken by about 14 s. Then a 'you' scenario, then a second concrete payoff at 20–30 s: the label's 'once a day, with or without food' and Lilly's 'any time of day' wording, each credited to its own source. Last comes a one-sentence open loop that pays off in the prescriber chapter.

scenes.narration: Starting orforglipron, the Foundayo pill? Here's what to expect in your first weeks and months.

visual.stock_query: hopeful person holding pill bottle, kitchen

scenes.retention_device: Direct question: names the drug and the title's exact promise in sentence 1

scenes.narration: Short answer: one pill a day. Stomach side effects like nausea are among the most common. And results are measured in months, not days.

items: Stomach side effects among most common

scenes.retention_device: Short answer delivered by about 14 s

scenes.narration: Picture day one. The bottle's on your counter, it's seven in the morning, and you're already running late. Do you need an empty stomach? A full glass of water?
Here's your first real answer. The prescribing information says one tablet a day, with or without food. And Lilly says it can be taken at any time of day, without food or water restrictions.
scenes.on_screen_text: Once a day, with or without food
scenes.retention_device: Second concrete payoff at 20–30 s (label wording plus Lilly's timing wording, each credited)

scenes.narration: So it can fit around your day. Stick around, because near the end there's one question for your prescriber that matters more than any timing rule.
scenes.retention_device: Open loop in one sentence, paid off in the prescriber chapter

scenes.narration: First, who this pill is actually for.

visual.stock_query: chapter card, teal gradient, pill icon

scenes.narration: The US FDA approved orforglipron, sold as Foundayo, in April twenty twenty-six. It's a GLP-1 medicine you swallow as a tablet, not an injection.
The label says it's for chronic weight management in adults with obesity, or in adults with overweight who also have at least one weight-related health condition.

items: Adults with overweight plus a weight-related condition
visual.stock_query: diverse adults in clinic waiting room

scenes.narration: It's meant to be used alongside a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity. So the pill is one part of the plan, not the whole plan.

visual.stock_query: pill, plate of vegetables, walking shoes

scenes.narration: Now, imagine someone. Let's call her Dana. She's forty-seven, and she's hypothetical, but maybe familiar. For years, comments at family dinners made her feel like this was all about willpower.

visual.stock_query: woman quiet at family dinner table, hurt

scenes.narration: If that's been you too, you're not alone. And asking your doctor about a medicine isn't giving up. It's asking a medical question.
scenes.retention_device: Name the feeling and validate it

scenes.narration: Here's a rule from the label that catches people out. Using Foundayo together with another GLP-1 medicine isn't recommended.
scenes.on_screen_text: Not recommended with other GLP-1 medicines

visual.stock_query: calm Medi holding stop hand, two medicine boxes

scenes.narration: So if you already use one, including a weekly injection, your prescriber needs to know before you start. Never combine them on your own.

visual.stock_query: person talking to prescriber at desk

scenes.narration: Okay, you know who it's for. Now let's get practical.
Next, how you actually take it.
It's a tablet, swallowed once a day, with or without food. And Lilly says any time of day works.

visual.stock_query: sun and moon around a clock, tablet

scenes.retention_device: Repeat payoff for viewers who joined late

scenes.narration: What about the dose? That's set by your prescriber, following the label, and it may change over time. We won't cover doses here, because that's their call, not a video's.
Here's a habit tip of our own, not from the label. Tie the pill to something you already do every day, like making coffee or plugging in your phone at night.

visual.stock_query: coffee mug next to phone charger, pill bottle

scenes.narration: If you're ever unsure what to do after a missed dose, check the Medication Guide that comes with your prescription, or ask your pharmacist.
And read that Medication Guide once, start to finish. It's written for patients, not doctors, and it lists the warning signs to watch for.

visual.stock_query: person reading leaflet on sofa, calm

scenes.narration: So taking it is simple. The harder question is what those first weeks actually feel like. And that's where the label's side effect table comes in.
scenes.on_screen_text: What do the first weeks feel like?

visual.stock_query: curious person looking at table chart

scenes.narration: Next: what your stomach may notice.
Picture Dana early on. Halfway through lunch, her stomach suddenly says: that's enough. Maybe she feels a little queasy, and she wonders if something's wrong.

visual.stock_query: woman at lunch, half plate, uneasy

scenes.narration: The prescribing information lists stomach and gut effects among the most common side effects. They include nausea, diarrhea, vomiting and constipation.
scenes.on_screen_text: Among the most common: stomach and gut

visual.stock_query: cartoon stomach with gentle wavy lines

scenes.narration: The label's table compares orforglipron with a placebo, a dummy pill, and these effects show up more often on the medicine. Worth knowing before you start.

visual.stock_query: two pill bottles on scale, comparison

scenes.narration: In the seventy-two-week trial in adults without diabetes, these stomach side effects were mostly mild to moderate.

visual.stock_query: gauge dial pointing low to middle

scenes.narration: But some people did stop. Over seventy-two weeks, about five to ten in every hundred people on orforglipron stopped because of side effects, depending on the dose. On placebo, it was about three in a hundred.
scenes.on_screen_text: Stopped for side effects, 72 weeks: about 5–10 in 100 on orforglipron vs about 3 on placebo

visual.stat_label: Orforglipron stopped for side effects, 72 weeks; placebo ~3
visual.stock_query: grid of 100 dots, a few highlighted

scenes.narration: Why does this happen at all? GLP-1 medicines slow down how quickly your stomach empties, and they act on appetite signals in the brain.
Food can stay in your stomach longer, so fullness may arrive sooner than you're used to. That's the feeling Dana noticed at lunch.
So what actually makes the early stretch easier? Here's what you can try, starting at your very next meal.
scenes.retention_device: New open loop before chapter change

scenes.narration: Making it easier. Quick note: these are general comfort tips from us, not label instructions, and your prescriber's advice comes first.
One. Eat smaller portions, and stop at the first sign of fullness, not at the bottom of the plate.

visual.stock_query: small plate of food, relaxed person

scenes.narration: Two. Slow down. Put your fork down between bites, and give your body a few minutes to register that it's had enough.

visual.stock_query: fork resting on plate, calm meal

scenes.narration: Three. While you're adjusting, go easy on very greasy, fried or heavy meals. Plain, simple foods may sit better.
Four. Drink fluids through the day, unless your doctor has told you to limit them. Small, regular sips count, especially after vomiting or diarrhea.

visual.stock_query: water glass refilled through the day

scenes.retention_device: Numbered tip, sets up kidney warning

scenes.narration: Five. If constipation shows up, fluids and fiber from foods like fruit, vegetables, beans and oats may help. Ask your pharmacist before adding any product.
And six. Tell your prescriber if side effects are severe or won't go away. You don't have to just push through and hope.
scenes.on_screen_text: 6. Severe or won't go away? Call

visual.stock_query: person calling clinic on phone, relieved

scenes.narration: For Dana, the biggest shift is in her head. She stops seeing a half-finished lunch as failure, and starts seeing it as information.
But Dana's real question is: what happens over months? The trial behind the approval answers that, in averages.
The results over seventy-two weeks.
The trial is called ATTAIN-1. It enrolled just over three thousand adults with obesity, or with overweight plus a weight-related condition. None of them had diabetes.

visual.stock_query: large diverse crowd of adults, trial

scenes.narration: Everyone got advice on healthier eating and physical activity. Then they were randomly assigned to orforglipron or a placebo pill, for seventy-two weeks.

visual.stock_query: two groups split by coin flip

scenes.narration: Here are the averages at week seventy-two. On the lowest dose: seven point five percent of body weight. On the highest dose: eleven point two percent. On placebo: two point one percent.

visual.stat_label: Average weight loss, 72 weeks, adults without diabetes

scenes.narration: To make that concrete: on the highest dose, for someone starting at two hundred pounds, about eleven percent is about twenty-two pounds. That's an average, so some people lost more and some lost less.
scenes.on_screen_text: Highest dose, on average: about 22 lb from 200 lb

visual.stock_query: bag of groceries beside a scale, neutral

scenes.narration: Those averages count everyone who was assigned to treatment, whether or not they kept taking it.

visual.stock_query: everyone in group counted, tally marks

scenes.narration: So the honest picture is gradual. If the scale barely moves in your second week, that isn't a verdict. The trial measured this in months.

visual.stock_query: person shrugging calmly at scale, sunrise

scenes.narration: And weight is one health measure among many. How you feel, how you move, what your doctor sees at your checkups: those count too.
Now, you may have seen headlines about orforglipron and sleep apnea. Those are trial results. Sleep apnea isn't an approved use of Foundayo.
scenes.on_screen_text: Sleep apnea: not an approved use

visual.stock_query: calm Medi beside newspaper, neutral face

scenes.retention_device: Re-hook from the news, scoped in one line

scenes.narration: The approved use is the one we covered at the start: weight management. Which brings us to the part you really shouldn't skip: the warnings.
The label's warnings. We'll go through them calmly. Knowing the real signs is what lets you stop worrying about everything else.

visual.stock_query: chapter card, neutral Medi with clipboard

scenes.narration: First, the boxed warning, about thyroid C-cell tumors. Other GLP-1 medicines caused these tumors in rodents. Orforglipron isn't active in rats or mice, and it didn't cause tumors in them. But it is active in people, and it isn't known whether it causes these tumors in humans. The label carries a boxed warning about them.

visual.stock_query: neutral Medi pointing at thyroid diagram

scenes.narration: Because of that, the label says not to use it if you or a family member has ever had medullary thyroid carcinoma, or M-T-C, or if you have M-E-N two, multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type two.

items: Personal or family history of MTC

scenes.narration: The Medication Guide says to tell your healthcare provider about a lump or swelling in your neck, trouble swallowing, hoarseness, or shortness of breath.

Second, pancreatitis. If you have severe pain in your stomach area that won't go away, with or without vomiting, stop taking it and call your healthcare provider right away. The pain may spread to your back.
scenes.on_screen_text: Severe stomach pain that won't go away: stop, call

visual.stock_query: person on phone to doctor, serious calm

scenes.narration: Third, gallbladder problems. Signs to call about include pain in your upper stomach, fever, yellowing of your skin or eyes, and clay-colored stools.
Fourth, dehydration and your kidneys. Losing fluid through vomiting or diarrhea can lead to dehydration, and the label warns that can cause kidney problems. That's why the fluids tip matters.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the earlier fluids tip

scenes.narration: Fifth, low blood sugar. The label says the risk is higher if you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea, a type of diabetes medicine. Signs can include dizziness, shakiness, sweating, confusion, hunger or a fast heartbeat.
scenes.on_screen_text: Insulin or sulfonylurea? Higher low-sugar risk

scenes.narration: Sixth, serious allergic reactions. If you get swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing, or a severe rash, stop taking it and get medical help right away.
scenes.on_screen_text: Serious allergic reaction: stop, get help

scenes.narration: And one line of context. In November twenty twenty-six, the FDA said it's requiring all GLP-1 medicine labels, Foundayo's included, to add a warning about a possible increased risk of NAY-on. That's a rare optic nerve condition that can cause sudden vision loss.
scenes.on_screen_text: FDA: possible NAION risk warning required for GLP-1 labels
scenes.retention_device: One neutral line of context on a topic viewers have heard about

scenes.narration: If you ever notice sudden vision loss, or part of your vision going missing, contact your healthcare provider right away.

visual.stock_query: person calling clinic, glasses on table

scenes.narration: For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop, switch or change your medicine on your own. Talk to your prescriber first.
scenes.on_screen_text: For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop, switch or change your medicine on your own. Talk to your prescriber first.

scenes.narration: That's the heavy part done, and you handled it. Now, the question I promised at the start.
scenes.retention_device: Main open loop about to pay off

scenes.narration: Questions for your prescriber.
Here it is. Tell your prescriber about every medicine you take: prescriptions, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins and supplements. The label has a whole section on drug interactions.
scenes.on_screen_text: Tell them every medicine you take

visual.stock_query: person laying out medicine boxes for doctor

scenes.narration: It's easy to forget, because a vitamin or a heartburn tablet doesn't feel like it counts. Mention it anyway. And always mention insulin or a sulfonylurea, because of that low blood sugar risk.
scenes.retention_device: Ties the payoff back to the warnings

scenes.narration: And if you use the birth control pill, tell your prescriber. The label says Foundayo may affect how well it works, and advises switching to a non-pill method, or adding a barrier method like condoms, for thirty days after starting and for thirty days after each dose increase.
scenes.on_screen_text: On the pill? Switch or add a barrier method: 30 days

visual.stock_query: calm woman with pill pack talking to doctor

scenes.retention_device: Surprising, practical interaction most viewers won't know

scenes.narration: Then ask: is this right for me, given my health history? How will we know it's working, and when should we check in?

items: How will we know it's working?

scenes.narration: Ask which side effects should make you call, and which can wait. And ask about any other GLP-1 medicine you're using or considering.

If you're pregnant, planning a pregnancy or breastfeeding, say so. And if you have surgery or a procedure with sedation coming up, ask what to tell that team. The label has a warning about anesthesia and deep sedation.
Imagine Dana walking in with that list on her phone. She isn't the patient who just nods anymore. She's a partner in her own care.

visual.stock_query: confident woman with phone list, doctor nodding

scenes.narration: Let's wrap it up into a checklist you can screenshot.
One pill a day, with or without food. Stomach side effects are among the most common. Smaller, slower meals. Fluids, unless you've been told to limit them.

scenes.narration: Know the emergency signs: severe stomach pain that won't go away, or a serious allergic reaction. Tell your prescriber every medicine you take. And judge progress in months, not days.

factcheck.summary:
Verdict: PASS, with three minor wording fixes. I found nothing that's wrong or unsafe.

I checked every factual claim against the July 2026 Foundayo prescribing information and Medication Guide (Lilly), the Lilly Medical approval page, the ACC journal scan and PubMed/NEJM summary of ATTAIN-1, and November 9, 2026 coverage of the FDA's NAION decision. The sleep apnea news is also confirmed.

Confirmed:
- **Approval and use:** FDA approval on April 1, 2026, for adults with obesity, or with overweight plus at least one weight-related condition. It's used with a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity.
- **How to take it:** once a day, with or without food. Lilly's "any time of day without food or water restrictions" wording is quoted from its press release and credited to Lilly.
- **Other GLP-1 medicines:** using it with one is not recommended.
- **Common side effects:** the gut effects listed match the label, and the label says it slows stomach emptying and acts on appetite areas of the brain.
- **ATTAIN-1:** 3,127 adults without diabetes. Average weight change at 72 weeks was 7.5%, 8.4% and 11.2% by dose, vs 2.1% on placebo. These averages count everyone assigned to treatment, which matches s45. Gut effects were mostly mild to moderate. 5–10% stopped because of side effects vs 3% on placebo. The 22 lb from 200 lb example is correct at 11.2%.
- **Warnings (label and Medication Guide):** pancreatitis (stop and call, pain may spread to the back), gallbladder signs, dehydration leading to kidney injury, low blood sugar with insulin or sulfonylureas, serious allergic reactions (stop and get help), and the anesthesia and deep sedation warning.
- **Birth control pills:** switch to a non-pill method or add a barrier method for 30 days after starting and 30 days after each dose increase. Foundayo's label says 30 days, not tirzepatide's 4 weeks, so the script is right.
- **NAION:** the FDA required the class-wide warning on Nov 9, 2026, and Foundayo is named in the list.
- **Sleep apnea:** the ATTAIN-OSA results are trial results only. It isn't an approved use.

Safety and framing are sound:
- The emergency stop instructions are scoped correctly, and the don't-stop line and the exact disclaimer plus prescriber line are present.
- There are no dosing details.
- Fluids carry a "unless told to limit" caveat, there's a pregnancy and breastfeeding prompt, and the low-blood-sugar caveat for insulin or sulfonylureas is there.
- The tips are clearly marked as ours, not the label's.
- Dana is clearly presented as hypothetical and isn't shamed.
- The hook pays off what the title promises.

Minor fixes:
1. **s51:** the explanation of the boxed warning is a paraphrase that goes slightly beyond the label's wording.
2. **s59:** should carry the FDA's "potential" and "rare" qualifiers.
3. **Sources:** the NAION claim cites trade press only.

**Source note:** I couldn't read the text of the S1 FDA PDF. It returned a real 1.1 MB PDF, so the link works, but I checked its content against the identical Lilly PI/Medication Guide (S2, revised July 2026). PubMed (S9) is behind a cookie wall for the fetch tool, but search confirmed the record and its numbers.

issues.claim: Orforglipron isn't active in rats or mice, so rodent studies can't show whether it would cause them, and it isn't known whether it causes these tumors in people. So the label carries the same warning.
issues.problem: The label says orforglipron 'is not pharmacologically active in rats or mice and did not produce tumors in rodents', and that the human relevance of these rodent tumors 'has not been determined'. 'So the label carries the same warning' is our own inference about why the warning is there, and it isn't stated in those words.
issues.fix: Narration: "First, the boxed warning, about thyroid C-cell tumors. Other GLP-1 medicines caused these tumors in rodents. Orforglipron isn't active in rats or mice, and it didn't cause tumors in them. But it is active in people, and it isn't known whether it causes these tumors in humans. The label carries a boxed warning about them."

issues.claim: the FDA said it's requiring all GLP-1 medicine labels, Foundayo's included, to add a warning about NAY-on, an optic nerve condition that can cause sudden vision loss.
issues.problem: The FDA describes this as a 'potential increased risk' of a 'rare' condition. Leaving out both qualifiers makes the line sound more certain and more alarming than the source.
issues.fix: Narration: "And one line of context. In November twenty twenty-six, the FDA said it's requiring all GLP-1 medicine labels, Foundayo's included, to add a warning about a possible increased risk of NAY-on. thumbnail.reasoning: All three are legible at phone size with a single clear focal point and no title-word repetition. #0 (\"FIRST MONTH? WEEK BY WEEK\") best matches the actual topic (an oral pill, \"what to expect\") by using a pill-bottle mascot instead of a generic body part, keeps a genuine curiosity gap (doesn't reveal what happens in month one), and the worried/uncertain expression matches the uncertainty implied by the question — no hard-cap violations. #1 (\"72 WKS\") is also clean and curiosity-preserving but the number is less central to \"what to expect\" in month one and the shocked face is a slightly generic reaction shot. #2 reuses the proven state-change nausea pattern, but the happy after-face edges toward visually answering \"yes, it's normal,\" and narrows a broad \"what to expect\" video to a single side effect, which slightly misleads about scope. #0 offers the strongest fit between packaging and content plus full legibility, so it's the best pick.
